title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
description: Find the shortest subarray with sum at least k, allowing negative numbers, using a monotonic deque of prefix-sum indices.

sections.title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K

content.title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums (which may contain negative numbers) and an integer k, return the length of the shortest non-empty contiguous subarray whose sum is at least k. Return -1 if no such subarray exists.

blocks.caption: A monotonic deque of prefix-sum indices finds, for every right endpoint, the closest valid left endpoint in O(1) amortized.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","nums[] (can contain negative numbers), k (target minimum sum)"],["Subarray","Contiguous, non-empty"],["Goal","Minimize length while sum >= k"],["Note","Negative numbers rule out a simple two-pointer sliding window, since the window sum is not monotonic as it grows"]]}

blocks.text: "Shortest subarray with sum at least k" over an array with negatives is a prefix-sum problem: subarray sum from j+1 to i equals prefix[i] - prefix[j]. Finding the shortest such subarray means, for each i, finding the LARGEST j < i with prefix[i] - prefix[j] >= k. A monotonic increasing deque of prefix indices maintains exactly the useful candidates for this search.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This extends the "prefix sum plus monotonic structure" idea from Jump Game VI and Constrained Subsequence Sum, but here the deque holds prefix INDICES ordered by prefix VALUE, not dp values, and both ends of the deque are actively used.

Picture a hiker tracking cumulative distance traveled (which can occasionally decrease if walking backward, hence negative array values). The hiker wants the shortest stretch of the walk covering at least k units of net forward distance. A checkpoint from earlier in the walk is only useful if its cumulative distance is smaller than a LATER checkpoint's, since a later, smaller cumulative distance would always give a shorter, equally valid or better stretch.

blocks.caption: Only checkpoints with strictly increasing cumulative distance are worth remembering.

items: prefix[i] - prefix[j] >= k (for j < i) means the subarray from index j to i-1 has sum at least k.

For a fixed i, the best (largest, closest) valid j is found among indices with the SMALLEST prefix values, since a smaller prefix[j] makes the difference bigger (easier to satisfy the sum condition) and, once found, using the LARGEST such j minimizes length.

A monotonic increasing deque of indices by prefix value keeps only "still useful" candidates: any index whose prefix value is not smaller than a later index's prefix value can never be the best choice again.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The shortest valid subarray has length 3, matching the expected output. It corresponds to the entire array [2,-1,2], whose sum is exactly 3.
A direct approach checks every pair (j, i) with j < i, computing prefix[i] - prefix[j] and tracking the minimum i - j among valid pairs. This is correct but quadratic.

The key structural insight for the speedup: for a fixed i, only indices j with a SMALLER prefix value than any later candidate can ever be useful, since a larger prefix[j] value makes the sum condition harder to satisfy without ever being closer (smaller i - j) either. This lets a monotonic increasing deque discard dominated indices from the back immediately, while the front is checked (and popped) whenever the current prefix minus the front is already big enough, since once satisfied, popping the front cannot help future i values find a SHORTER length either.
Compute prefix sums, then check every pair (j, i) with j < i directly for the sum condition, tracking the minimum valid length.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n^2)","Every pair (j, i) is checked directly"],["Space","O(n)","The prefix sum array"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Most pairs are irrelevant, since a j with a larger prefix value than some later j' can never be the useful choice once j' is available, but the brute force still checks them all.

Maintain a monotonic increasing deque of prefix-sum indices. For each i, first pop from the FRONT while the current prefix minus the front prefix satisfies the sum condition, recording the length each time (the front is always the best/closest valid j once found, so popping it is safe and correct). Then pop from the BACK any indices whose prefix value is greater than or equal to the current one, since they can never be a better choice than the current index going forward. Finally push the current index.

items: Build the prefix sum array, O(n).
For each i, pop front while prefix[i] - prefix[front] >= k, recording i - front each time.
Pop back while prefix[back] >= prefix[i] (dominated), then push i.
Subarray sum problems, especially with negative numbers, are naturally rephrased in terms of prefix sum differences.
When the array can contain negatives, a two-pointer sliding window is unsound (window sum is not monotonic); a monotonic deque of prefix indices is the correct generalization.
Popping from both ends of the deque serves different purposes: the front pop finds and records valid answers, while the back pop discards indices that can never be useful again.

blocks.text: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K is solved by rephrasing the sum condition as a prefix-sum difference, then using a monotonic increasing deque of prefix indices: front pops find and record valid shortest lengths, and back pops discard indices dominated by a smaller, later prefix value, giving an O(n) solution that correctly handles negative numbers.
